gloss: thick cloud, drip like rain; nape, break the neck
summary:
The thick cloud in David’s song belongs to the description of Yahweh coming down. The shorter noun occurs in Isaiah, where it also obscures the light.

The nape is visible when someone turns away. Hebrew draws on this posture to describe both retreat from a pursuer and a refusal to listen.

senses.definition: David describes the cloud beneath Yahweh’s feet as he descends. At Sinai Moses draws near to the thick darkness, while the people remain at a distance. Job pictures gloom as the wrapping of the newborn sea.
Isaiah describes light obscured by clouds at the close of a picture of distress and darkness over the land.
Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain and his speech like dew. In his blessing Israel’s skies drip dew.
The owner must break the neck of a firstborn donkey left unredeemed. The elders break a heifer’s neck in the prescribed inquiry into an unsolved killing. Hosea applies the verb to destroying altars.

senses.gloss: nape or back turned in flight
senses.definition: Jacob pictures Judah’s hand on the neck of his enemies. David thanks Yahweh for giving him his enemies’ backs as they flee.
Israel is called stiff-necked after making the calf. Jeremiah joins stiffening the neck to refusing to listen.

evidence.locator: Book I p. 2014, n28734, mane or hair on the ridge of the neck

note:
The Akkadian cloud word offers a possible parallel for the shorter Hebrew noun. The formation of the longer עֲרָפֶל and its relationship to the verb for dripping remain uncertain.

The Arabic mane word names the hair along the neck and offers a possible comparison. The Hebrew noun itself designates the back of the neck.
